common_name: Fragrans Skimmia (Heirloom Fragrant Male Pollinator Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Fragrans is an older male Skimmia selection grown chiefly as a fragrant pollinator for female berry-producing cultivars, predating the more compact 'Kew Green'.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, where this long-established male Skimmia selection tolerates deeper shade than most flowering evergreens. Fragrans forms a rounded, somewhat looser mound than 'Kew Green' and is grown almost entirely for its dense clusters of small, intensely sweet-scented white spring flowers rather than for foliage compactness, making it a favorite near paths and doorways where the fragrance can be enjoyed at close range. As a male clone it sets no berries itself but is an effective, wide-ranging pollinator for nearby female Skimmia japonica cultivars grown for their red winter fruit. Keep soil consistently moist, mulch to preserve acidity, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Bowles' Dwarf Female Skimmia (Compact Heavy-Berrying Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; site a male pollinator such as 'Rubella' or 'Kew Green' within about 15 feet, since Bowles' Dwarf Female needs cross-pollination to set its heavy berry crop despite its diminutive size.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Bowles' Dwarf Female is a compact selection prized for producing a disproportionately heavy crop of bright red berries on a notably small, dense frame, making it one of the best Skimmia choices for small gardens, foundation plantings, and containers where full-size female cultivars would be too large. Small, fragrant, creamy-white spring flower clusters open above glossy, leathery evergreen foliage and are followed by long-persisting berries once pollinated by a nearby male. Water during dry spells and mulch to keep the root zone evenly moist and acidic, and prune only lightly to remove damaged growth, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Somerset grows larger and more vigorously than 'Carol Mackie' and bears plain green foliage rather than a variegated margin.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun; Daphne resents root disturbance, so choose a permanent site from the start. Somerset is one of the larger and more vigorous Daphne x burkwoodii selections, forming a rounded, semi-evergreen shrub with plain blue-green foliage rather than the creamy variegation of 'Carol Mackie', and in mid-spring it produces an especially heavy flush of small, intensely fragrant pale pink flowers that can perfume a wide area. Its bigger mature size suits it to a mixed shrub border or as a specimen where its scent and floral display have room to make an impact. Avoid heavy pruning and wet feet, both poorly tolerated by Daphne; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Albert Burkwood Daphne (Original Fragrant Hybrid Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Albert Burkwood was the original selection from the 1930s Daphne caucasica x Daphne cneorum cross from which the whole burkwoodii group of garden hybrids descends.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade with shelter from harsh afternoon sun; choose a permanent site at planting time, since Daphne resents root disturbance. Albert Burkwood is the original Daphne x burkwoodii selection, raised in England in the early 1930s and the parent of the whole burkwoodii group of garden hybrids, forming a dense, rounded, semi-evergreen shrub with narrow, faintly gray-green leaves. In mid to late spring it bears abundant clusters of small, pale pink, sweetly fragrant flowers, with a lighter scattered rebloom sometimes occurring later in summer. Avoid heavy pruning and waterlogged soil, both poorly tolerated by Daphne; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fall planting also succeeds in mild climates.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and pull off tattered older leaves by tugging them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Overture is a Blooms of Bressingham-raised Bergenia hybrid valued for its saturated deep rose-crimson flower clusters, held on sturdy red stems well above rounded, glossy, leathery leaves that flush bronze-red through winter cold. Its compact, tidy habit suits the front of shaded borders, path edging, and mixed containers alongside hostas and ferns. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

common_name: Winterglut Bergenia (Winter Fire, Deep Carmine-Red Pigsqueak)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Winterglut ('Winter Fire') is a German-bred, RHS Award of Garden Merit hybrid, distinct from the Terra Nova selection 'Winterglow' already in this dataset.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and pull off tattered older leaves by tugging them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Winterglut (German for 'winter fire') was raised by the Arends nursery in Germany and holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its compact habit and richly saturated carmine-red flower clusters, opening on red stems in early spring above rounded, leathery leaves that deepen to a strong burgundy through winter cold. Its dense, relatively low profile makes it a reliable choice for the front of shaded borders and mass plantings where consistent winter color is wanted. Divide crowded clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Purpurea is a long-established, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of the straight species with larger leaves and richer flower color than most modern compact hybrids.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and pull off tattered older leaves by tugging them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Purpurea is a long-cultivated selection of Bergenia cordifolia carrying a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, bearing large, rounded, leathery leaves and dense clusters of rich magenta-purple flowers on thick, upright stems in early to mid-spring, ahead of most other bergenia selections. Its coarser, bolder leaves and exceptional cold hardiness make it a good choice for mass plantings and large-scale groundcover in colder climates where finer hybrid cultivars struggle. Divide crowded clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

common_name: Chocolate Wing Rodgersia (Dark Chocolate-Bronze Foliage Rodgersia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chocolate Wing has the darkest, most consistently chocolate-toned foliage of the podophylla cultivars, holding its color from spring emergence through fall.

directions: Plant in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, along a pond edge or damp woodland bed. Chocolate Wing produces large, deeply lobed, duck-foot-shaped leaves that emerge a rich, dark chocolate-red in spring, hold much of that bronze-red cast through summer, and deepen again in autumn, giving it more sustained dark color than the greener-summer forms of the species. Airy, astilbe-like plumes of creamy-white to pale pink flowers rise above the foliage in early to midsummer. Give it a sheltered site out of drying wind, since the large, thin leaves scorch and tatter quickly if soil moisture lapses; mulch generously to hold moisture and keep the foliage color at its richest.
